title: AI copyright: Product purpose reshapes market harm
desc: Examines public law, editorial expression, transformativeness and substitution without treating AI training as categorically lawful or unlawful.

kps.k: The debate turns on the particular copying, product function and protected market—not whether AI training is categorically lawful.
kps.d: The ROSS district court rejected fair use for training a competing, non-generative legal-search tool. Bartz found specific LLM-training copies fair, while Kadrey granted Meta a record-specific victory on thirteen authors’ reproduction claims. These outcomes distinguish retrieval that substitutes for an existing research service from multipurpose generation, but do not establish a universal generative-versus-non-generative rule. The ROSS appeal remains pending in the supplied account.

kps.k: Legal-information copyright separates public law from editorial expression, but the extent of that separation remains contested.
kps.d: Bibas finds originality in Westlaw’s selection and arrangement, individual headnotes and Key Number System, while excluding judicial opinions themselves from protection. ROSS argues that accurate restatement of legal holdings leaves little or no protectable expression. Copyrightability does not resolve fair use: the district court gives ROSS factor two because the editorial material has limited creativity, and factor three because users receive no headnotes. Bartz and Kadrey likewise recognize expressive book content while allowing complete copying where reasonably related to the training purpose.

qs.q: Now I see no genuine dispute that  the headnotes and Key Number System clear Feist’s minimal threshold for originality.

kps.k: Transformativeness depends on whether courts emphasize the internal training operation or the resulting product’s purpose.
kps.d: ROSS characterizes its headnote-derived training as intermediate copying that teaches question-to-opinion matching without displaying protected headnotes. Applying Warhol, Bibas instead emphasizes the shared legal-research purpose and distinguishes software reverse-engineering precedents. Bartz and Kadrey treat generation of new, diverse text as a different purpose from reading the source books. Neither commerciality nor an absence of reproduced source text alone decides fair use; Bartz also assumes the authors’ memorisation argument without treating that assumption as dispositive.

qs.q: It used headnote-derived training examples to teach a machine-learning system how to match legal questions to relevant passages in judicial opinions.

kps.k: Market definition divides protection against copyright injury from protection against ordinary competition.
kps.d: The ROSS opinion treats intended substitution for Westlaw and potential training-data licensing as harms favoring Thomson Reuters. On appeal, ROSS argues that the inquiry should concern protected headnote expression, not the incumbent’s business generally, and warns that recognizing a licence for every contested use makes fair use circular. Taylor acknowledges that risk but cautions that a standalone-headnote market ignores bundled subscriptions. Bartz and Kadrey reject the asserted training-licensing entitlement for the uses before them; Bartz does so even assuming a licensing market could develop, rather than finding such a market economically impossible.

qs.q: And it does not matter whether Thomson Reuters has used the data to train its  own legal search tools; the effect on a potential market for AI training data is enough.
qs.a: Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. ROSS Intelligence Inc. — Memorandum Opinion on Renewed Summary Judgment (D. Del., Bibas, J.) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: ROSS resisted defining the market as “AI training” or “legal research platforms,” warning that doing so would make fair use circular: any innovative use could be converted into a licensing market simply because the copyright owner, after seeing the use, says it would have licensed that use.
qs.a: Thomson Reuters v. ROSS Intelligence at the Third Circuit — Interlocutory Appeal No. 25-2153, Argued 11 June 2026 (Decision Pending) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Kadrey’s market-dilution reasoning challenges the view that non-infringing outputs necessarily avoid cognizable market harm.
kps.d: Bartz distinguishes original authorship from insulation against competing works. Kadrey argues that AI’s capacity to generate vast numbers of genre- or subject-matter competitors could undermine authors’ markets even without substantial similarity, and criticizes Bartz’s analogy to human learning. That warning is not a finding of dilution: Meta supplied expert evidence of no discernible sales effect shortly after Llama 3’s release, while the authors supplied no contrary empirical evidence. Kadrey’s prediction that better-supported plaintiffs may win remains dictum, not proof of present or inevitable harm.

kps.k: Acquisition, retention, digitisation and training require distinct analysis rather than a single justification for the entire data pipeline.
kps.d: Bartz permits replacement digitisation where Anthropic destroyed purchased print originals and did not redistribute the digital replacements. It separately rejects fair use for a pirated general-purpose library, supported by employee statements about indefinite retention even of books never selected for training. Kadrey rejects unauthorized acquisition as an automatic defeat, evaluating downloading in light of its training purpose while leaving distribution claims live. The practical implication is to document provenance, copying purposes, retention and distribution separately; a favorable training ruling does not necessarily resolve other uses.

kps.k: Procedural posture and evidentiary limits constrain claims about what the ROSS litigation establishes.
kps.d: Early reporting records Judge Stark’s skepticism about allegations and Thomson Reuters’ plausible-inference response, not a finding that copying did or did not occur. The later Bibas opinion compares memo questions, headnotes and judicial text individually, finding copying and substantial similarity for 2,243 headnotes while preserving copyright-validity and other factual disputes. Its illustrative table is not record evidence. On appeal, ROSS challenges summary judgment and Thomson Reuters defends the absence of material disputes. Taylor’s reading of skeptical appellate questions is commentary, not a decided outcome.

kps.k: The practical stakes concern access to legal information, incentives for curation and the cost of lawful AI development.
kps.d: Access-oriented ROSS amici warn that broad headnote protection could entrench legal-information incumbents; copyright-owner amici warn that a non-reproducing-output exemption could undermine curated-content licensing. Lee, who joined an amicus brief supporting ROSS, treats UpCodes’ preliminary-injunction fair-use analysis as especially favorable; Taylor leaves the analogy open and recommends expression-, function- and market-specific analysis. Independent creation, licensing and public-domain material emerge as possible development routes, not guarantees of commercial feasibility. Predictions that copyright enforcement will halt innovation—or merely slow it—remain contested forecasts.

qs.q: The Free Law Project and legal tech amici make a similar point in more market-oriented terms: overbroad protection for headnotes can entrench incumbents and chill legal technology development.

vlens.an:
These selected regulators-and-courts sources collectively accept the proposition that AI-training copyright questions turn on the particular copying, resulting product, protected market and evidentiary record—not on a categorical rule for AI. They also materially develop it. The ROSS court and related commentary focus on the shared legal-research purpose, direct substitution for Westlaw and a potential training-data market, while expressly limiting the ruling to the non-generative system before the court. Bartz differentiates generative training from competing opinion retrieval and further separates training, replacement digitisation and retention of a pirated general-purpose library, requiring an independent justification for each use. Kadrey likewise insists on case-specific adjudication but adds that even highly transformative training could lose where evidence shows product-level market dilution from mass-generated competing works.

The principal internal variation concerns what counts as cognizable market harm and how acquisition relates to training. ROSS recognizes both substitution and a potential training-data licensing market; Bartz rejects a claimed entitlement to control the training market for the use before it; and Kadrey rejects that licensing theory on its record while treating indirect market dilution as potentially actionable. Bartz treats pirated-library retention as a separately unjustified use, whereas Kadrey does not regard shadow-library acquisition as an automatic defeat and evaluates downloading in light of its overall training purpose. These are materially different applications of a shared fact-, function- and market-specific framework, rather than disagreement with the proposition. Because this is a curated set, the synthesis characterizes only these sources and does not establish the prevalence of this view among regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: CONCLUSION  Fair use is a fact-specific doctrine that requires case-by-case analysis that is sensitive to new technologies and their potential consequences.

vlens.an: This legal-tech-vendor source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI-training copyright disputes should turn on the particular expression copied, the use’s function, substitution and the legally cognizable copyright market—not on a categorical rule for AI training. Taylor’s preferred approach closely tracks that proposition: ordinary, fact-specific fair-use analysis that distinguishes harm to protected expression and its market from ordinary competition with an incumbent’s broader business. The source also reinforces the cluster’s caution against generalising from ROSS, because ROSS involved an unusual direct-competitor legal-search product rather than general-purpose generative AI. There is material internal variation within the combined source: Taylor presents competing access, curation and licensing interests and leaves the outcome and UpCodes analogy open, whereas Lee is more affirmatively favorable to ROSS, treating UpCodes and access to law as especially strong support. That difference concerns how the case-specific balance should be resolved, not whether the governing analysis should be context-sensitive. As this is one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: It would say that AI training is not automatically fair use and not automatically infringement.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI-training copyright outcomes depend on the particular copying, resulting product function, protected market and evidentiary record, rather than on a categorical rule. They also materially develop that proposition. The ROSS opinion and commentary focus on a non-generative legal-research product intended to substitute for Westlaw, while expressly limiting the ruling’s broader reach. Bartz distinguishes generative training from competing opinion retrieval and extends the analysis across separate stages of the data pipeline: training, replacement digitisation and retention of a pirated general-purpose library each require their own justification. Kadrey adds a further product-level inquiry—whether mass-generated outputs could indirectly dilute source markets—but treats that harm as a possibility requiring evidence, not as an established consequence of LLM training. Material internal variation concerns market definition and acquisition: ROSS recognizes substitution and a potential training-data licensing market; Bartz rejects entitlement to such a licensing market for the training use before it and finds pirated-library retention unfair; Kadrey also rejects the asserted licensing entitlement on its record but does not treat shadow-library acquisition as automatically dispositive. Kadrey’s expectation that stronger market-dilution evidence may change future outcomes is dictum and prediction, whereas Meta’s victory rests on the plaintiffs’ evidentiary failure. Thus, the period’s sources reinforce the cluster’s central framework while adding distinct-use, provenance and proof-sensitive dimensions; they should not be read as representing all courts or commentators.

elens.an: The 2026 source accepts the cluster’s principal proposition: AI-training copyright disputes should turn on the particular expression copied, the use’s function, product substitution and the relevant copyright market, rather than on a categorical rule that training is always fair use or always infringement. It reinforces the proposition by treating ROSS as an unusual direct-competitor legal-search case whose outcome should not automatically govern general-purpose generative AI. There is material internal variation within the source: Lee is more favorable to ROSS, emphasizing UpCodes and access to law, while Taylor reads the appellate panel as skeptical of ROSS and gives greater weight to direct competition, editorial value and potentially legitimate licensing interests. That variation concerns how the case-specific factors should apply, not whether a fact-specific framework is needed, so the overall position remains supportive rather than mixed.
